note: Messages in bottles (docs/future/12): bottles are the only made things the sea brings to the shore, and some hold a letter. Set 1 is Matt's own 40 (October 21, 2026), standing in until his writer friend's arrive; add new sets to letters with new ids. A letter comes in a bottle of its rarity or rarer, in its season (or any), only after the letter it answers (after) has been read, and lateGame ones only once the island is lateGameDays old. Unread letters come first. The body uses light markup: **bold**, ~~struck~~, *italic*, and lines starting # or ## as headings; an empty line is a paragraph break. Voice: warm first, wistful second; the outside world distant and unnamed; no plot.

letters.title: Lantern Float Postponed
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER**
### LANTERN FLOAT POSTPONED FOR FOG
#### Organizers say the weather "simply didn't ask"
The forty-first Lowmarsh Lantern Float, planned for Saturday evening, has been postponed after a fog bank settled over the harbor shortly before dusk and showed no sign of leaving.
"We had two hundred lanterns ready," said committee chair Odette Brill. "You couldn't see your own hand. Sending lanterns into that would have been like mailing letters into a pillow."
Some residents went ahead anyway. Witnesses report at least a dozen small lights drifting out past the breakwater around nine o'clock, though no one will admit to launching them.
The float has been moved to the next clear night. The committee asks residents to keep their lanterns dry and their expectations modest.
*Also in this issue: The bakery on Tern Street reopens after its oven "took a long rest." A reader writes in about an unusually polite heron. Tide tables, page 6.*

letters.title: Nan's Kelp Bread
body: **Nan's Kelp Bread**
*Makes one loaf, or two small arguments.*
- 3 cups flour, whatever kind is in the tin
- 1 handful dried kelp, crumbled fine (the brown kind, not the slippery kind)
- 1 spoon honey
- salt, but less than you think, the kelp is already salty
- warm water, until the dough feels like an earlobe
Knead until your mind wanders off and comes back. Let it rise somewhere it can see the window. Bake until the kitchen smells like the shore at low tide, but in a good way.
Eat warm with butter. Do not share with gulls, no matter what they tell you.

letters.title: Dear Wren
body: Dear Wren,
The ferry doesn't stop here anymore, so I'm trying the old way.

I planted the quince you gave me on the south side, where you said. It sulked for two years, and then all at once it decided to be a tree. There are blossoms on it now. I keep meaning to count them and keep losing track, which I think is the right amount of blossoms.
The house is quiet but not empty, if you understand the difference. I think you do. That was always the thing about you.
Come in spring if the boats run. If they don't, write. If you can't write, I'll assume the sea has the letter and is taking the long way round.
Your sister,
Ada

letters.title: Keeper's Log
letters.form: A page torn from a larger book
body: **Keeper's Log — Saltbarrow Light**
**3rd.** Wind NW, moderate. Lamp lit 5:40. Seal on the lower rocks again. Have named him Councillor.
**4th.** Fog. Horn sounded through the night. Councillor unbothered.
**5th.** Clear. Painted the north rail. Ran out of white halfway, so the north rail is now two colors. Will call it a design choice.
**6th.** Nothing passed. Lit the lamp anyway. That's the job.
**7th.** Councillor brought a friend.

letters.title: Before the Boat Left
letters.form: List on the back of a receipt
body: Things I meant to say before the boat left:
1. Thank you for the scarf.
2. I did know it was you who fixed the gate.
3. The song you hum while you wash the dishes — I hum it now too. I don't know the words. I don't think you do either.
4. I'll be back when the plums are ripe.
5. Water the plums.

letters.title: To the Gull
body: To the gull who took my sandwich on the pier last Tuesday,
I shouted some things I'm not proud of. You were hungry and I wasn't paying attention, and that isn't a crime, it's a Tuesday.
I hope it was good. It had cucumber in it.
No hard feelings,
The man in the yellow hat
P.S. If this reaches a different gull, please pass it along.

letters.title: Sixty Years of Birds
body: **THE GERROW POINT GAZETTE**
### LOCAL WOMAN, 91, FINISHES SIXTY-YEAR COUNT OF HEADLAND BIRDS
#### "I'm sure I missed a few," she says
For sixty years, Marguerite Ostby has walked the same path along Gerrow Headland every morning with a notebook and a pencil, writing down every bird she saw.
On Tuesday she wrote her last entry, closed the final notebook (the one hundred and twelfth) and declared the count complete.

"It isn't that I'm tired of birds," she said from her kitchen, where the notebooks fill two shelves and part of a third. "It's that I've seen enough of them to know they'll carry on without me writing it down."
Her records, which note weather, tide and, on one occasion, "a gull with a grudge," have been offered to the town library. The librarian called them extraordinary, and in places very funny.
Asked what she would do with her mornings now, Mrs. Ostby said she planned to walk the same path, without the notebook.
"I'd like to see what I notice when I'm not counting."

letters.title: Keeping a Garden While Away
letters.form: Instructions, numbered in a looping hand
body: **How to keep a garden while you're away**
1. Plant things that don't need you. They're out there, and they're kinder than the needy ones.
2. Mulch thickly. Think of it as tucking them in.
3. Leave one corner wild. Something will move in, and it will be glad.
4. Tell the garden you're leaving. It won't understand, but you'll feel better.
5. When you come back, don't fix everything at once. Walk around first. See what it did without you. It's usually more than you'd expect.

letters.title: To Whoever Tends the Next Island
body: To whoever tends the next island,
I've been here a long time. Long enough that the herons stopped leaving when I walk past, and the frogs sing whether I'm listening or not. That took years. It was worth every one of them.
I'm going soon. Not far. There's a smaller island past the reef with nothing on it but sand and a stubborn little pine. I'd like to start again. I'd like to be bad at it again.
A few things I learned:
The crabs like their sand piled, not flat.
Turn over the stones, but put them back the way you found them.
Don't try to keep everything. Keep the things that made you stop.
And when the island doesn't need you as much anymore — one day it won't — that isn't a sign you did something wrong. It's the whole point.
Look after it.
Or rather, let it look after itself, and keep it company.
letters.hook: Suggested placement: only after the player has tended the island for a long stretch, as a quiet nod toward the farewell-and-sister-island ending.

letters.title: Dear Ada
body: Dear Ada,
Your letter reached me in the end, which I'm told is unusual, so I'm choosing to take it as a sign.

I can't come in spring. The boats only run when they feel like it, and lately they don't feel like it. But I'll come in summer if I have to row, and you know I'm terrible at rowing, so plan for me to arrive late and blistered.
I'm glad the quince decided. I knew it would. Things usually do, if you leave them alone long enough and don't stare.
Quiet but not empty. Yes. I understand exactly.
Save me a blossom, or a quince if I'm very late.
Wren

letters.title: The Last Crossing
body: **THE SALTBARROW TIDINGS**
### OUTER ISLES FERRY MAKES FINAL CROSSING
#### Captain rings the bell "for everyone who ever missed it"
After eighty-one years, the ferry *Patience* made her final crossing to the outer isles on Sunday, carrying four passengers, eleven crates of post and a goat whose ownership remains unclear.
Service ends as fewer families stay on the islands year-round. The harbor board says a smaller boat will make deliveries "when the weather and the tide agree."

Captain Ilse Varn, who has worked the route for thirty years, rang the ship's bell three times as she left the outer quay. Asked why, she said it was for everyone who had ever run down the pier just too late.
"There were a lot of them," she said. "I always waited a little."
The *Patience* will be retired to the boatyard, where volunteers hope to repaint her by spring. The goat has been offered a home at the lighthouse.

letters.title: Classifieds
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER — CLASSIFIEDS**
**LOST:** One left boot, brown, near the breakwater. Right boot very lonely. Inquire at the chandlery.
**FOUND:** Small wooden boat, painted green, name rubbed off. Floats well. Seems to have been loved.
**FOR SALE:** Accordion, lightly used. Seller's neighbors say heavily used. Offers welcome.
**WANTED:** Someone to teach a stubborn old man to swim. Patience required. Biscuits provided.
**FREE:** Kittens, four. Three are sensible. One will climb your curtains. You will love that one most.
**NOTICE:** To whoever keeps leaving fresh bread on the chapel step: thank you. We don't know who you are. Please don't stop.

letters.title: Margins of a Tide Table
letters.form: A printed tide table, the numbers mostly faded, with notes in the margins
body: **4th.** Lowest tide of the year. Walked out to the far sandbar. Found a starfish the size of a dinner plate. Put it back.
**11th.** High tide reached the third step. Mother says it used to reach the fifth.
**17th.** Missed low tide. Slept in. Worth it.
**23rd.** Spring tide. Moon enormous. Didn't need the lamp.
**30th.** The numbers on this page are guesses the sea has agreed to, mostly.

letters.title: When I Grow Up
body: **What I Want to Be When I Grow Up**
by Ottilie, Class 3
When I grow up I want to be a lighthouse. Not the keeper. The lighthouse.

I would stand on the rocks and be very tall and never get tired. Ships would see me and think, there is Ottilie, we are nearly home. At night I would be very bright, and in the day I would just be a nice building for birds.
The only bad thing is I could not go to the beach, because I would be at the beach already, all the time, so actually that is fine.
The end.
*In red pencil, at the bottom:*
A lovely ambition. Please see me about the difference between "be" and "become." Also, I think you would make a very good lighthouse.

letters.title: Hush Now
body: Hush now, the boats are all home in the bay,
the gulls have stopped arguing over the day,
the moon's on the water, the water's asleep,
and nothing is out there too far or too deep.
Hush now, the lamp in the window is low,
the tide's going out, but it's slow, it's so slow,
and whatever it carries away in the night,
it brings something back with the first of the light.

letters.title: Dear Pip
body: Dear Pip,
I am not a whale. I'm sorry. I'm a retired net-mender with a bad knee, which is nearly as good.

I have been to the middle of the ocean, once, a long time ago. It is very wide and very blue and very quiet, and at night there are more stars than you'd think there was room for. Mostly it is the same as the edges, only more so.
I did see a whale. It looked at me for a long time and then went on with its day. I think that's what whales do.
I hope your tooth came out and you got something for it.
Abel, across the water
P.S. I won't tell your mum about the bottle. But you should probably tell her yourself. Mums like that.

letters.title: Log of the *Little Margin*
letters.form: A page from a small sailboat's log
body: **Day 1.** Left harbor. Wind fair. Feeling brave.
**Day 3.** Wind gone. Feeling less brave.
**Day 4.** Still no wind. Read the only book on board for the second time. The ending is different when you're becalmed.
**Day 6.** Wind back. Dolphins for an hour. Forgave the sea for everything.
**Day 9.** Land in sight. Not the land I was aiming for. Going anyway. Seems nice.

letters.title: To Me, in Ten Years
body: To me, in ten years,
I hope you still walk before breakfast.
I hope you fixed the roof, or made peace with the bucket.
I hope you stopped saying "one day" about the things you really meant.
If you didn't, that's all right. Here's a reminder, delivered very slowly.
— You, younger and a little worried

letters.title: A Polite Heron
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER — LETTERS**
### A Polite Heron
Sir,

I write to report that the heron at the bottom of Mill Lane has, for three mornings running, stepped aside on the path to let me pass. On the third morning it inclined its head. I inclined mine back. I don't know what we agreed to, but I intend to honor it.
I mention this only because so few people on Mill Lane do the same.
Yours, etc.,
R. Dunmore, Mill Lane
*Editor's note: We have since received two further letters about this heron, both confirming it is very polite.*

letters.title: About the Fog
body: About the fog, and the Lantern Float.
It was me. Well, me and eleven others, it turns out. None of us planned it. We each went down to the water with one lantern, thinking we'd be the only one.
You couldn't see anything. But you could see the lights. Twelve of them, going out together.
I've never told anyone. Now I've told the sea. That feels about right.

body: **Keeper's Log — Saltbarrow Light**
**8th.** Councillor's friend still here. Larger than Councillor. Have named her Alderman.
**9th.** Gale. Lamp lit 4:50. Both seals on the lower rocks, facing the weather like two old men at a bus stop.

letters.title: The Boot
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER — CLASSIFIEDS**
**FOUND:** One left boot, brown, washed up at Pell's Cove. Has clearly been somewhere. A small crab is living in the toe and would prefer not to be disturbed.
**WANTED:** The owner of the lonely right boot. Your left boot is safe, and frankly doing better than ever.
**FOR SALE:** Accordion. Second notice. Price reduced. Neighbors have offered to chip in.

letters.title: Dear Wren, Once More
letters.form: Letter, a third, the same careful hand
body: Dear Wren,
Your letter came. It took the long way round, just as I said it might, and arrived smelling faintly of tar, which I have decided is the smell of distance.
The quince gave eleven fruit this year. I made jam with nine of them and set the other two on the windowsill, because they were too handsome to cook. The kitchen smells like your old room.
I've stopped waiting at the jetty. Not because I've stopped hoping. I just realised the jetty doesn't need me standing on it for a boat to come.
Come when you can. The second bed is made. It has been made for a while.
Ada

body: Monday: a blue rope, good as new
Tuesday: one shoe for a very small person

Thursday: a gull feather, perfectly fine
Friday: three of something I can't name

letters.title: Night Shift

letters.title: For Whoever Feeds Moth
letters.form: Instructions for a cat-sitter, numbered, two coffee rings
body: 1. Her name is Moth. She will not answer to it.
2. Breakfast at seven. She will tell you it is six. It is not six.
3. She sleeps on the warm end of the stove. Let her.
4. If she brings you a present, say thank you and put it outside when she isn't looking.
5. She likes the radio on low. Anything but the shipping forecast, which she finds upsetting.
6. Do not let her out after dark. She will argue. Be firm, then give in a little.
7. Thank you. I'll be back before the moon is full. Tell her I said so. She won't believe you either.

letters.title: Fog Soup
body: **FOG SOUP** (serves however many come in from the cold)
One onion, cut slowly.
Whatever is left in the bottom of the basket.
A handful of barley, for patience.
Water, enough to cover your worries.
Salt from the shore.
Simmer until the windows go white. Stir when someone tells a story. Serve when the fog is thickest and nobody is going anywhere.

letters.title: Weather Corner
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER**
### WEATHER CORNER
**Today:** Grey, then greyer. A brief bright spell around noon, for anyone who happens to look up.
**Tonight:** Wind from the west. Hang on to your washing and your opinions.
**Tomorrow:** Uncertain. Our forecaster has gone out in the boat to have a closer look.
*Readers are reminded that the weather has never once consulted this column.*

letters.title: An Apology to a Heron
body: Dear Heron,
I am sorry I sneezed. You had been standing so still, for so long, and you were so nearly about to catch something.
You gave me a look I will remember for the rest of my life.
I have brought a handkerchief every day since. It has not helped our relationship, but it has helped me.
Respectfully, from the bank

letters.title: The Other Corner
letters.form: A second torn corner of a hand-drawn map: open water, a compass rose, and one small island drawn with great care
body: *Written along the torn edge:*
If you have the other piece, you'll know the marks weren't treasure.
This is the part I kept. It's where we said we'd meet if we ever got lost: the little island with nobody on it.
I never went. I like knowing it's there. Somebody should be on it, I think. Somebody kind.
*And underneath, smaller:* If that's you, hello.

letters.title: From the Back Row
letters.form: Letter, on a choir's program, written up the side
body: To whoever finds this,
We sang tonight in the harbor hall, all forty of us, and the roof leaked onto the altos, and nobody stopped.
I sing in the back row because I can't hold a note on my own. In the middle of forty people I can. I think that's the best thing I know about people.
I'm putting the program in a bottle because I don't want to throw it away and I don't want to keep it in a drawer. This seemed like the third choice.
Second bass, back row, very happy

letters.title: Seed Swap
letters.form: A notice, pinned once, the pin hole rusted
body: ## SEED SWAP
### Chapel steps, first fine Saturday
Bring what you saved. Take what you need. Label your packets, or don't, and let it be a surprise.
Last year somebody's "sweet peas" came up as an enormous squash. We are still talking about it. We are grateful.
*Tea provided. Bring your own cup. Bring a story about something that grew.*

letters.title: Overheard on the Ferry
letters.form: Scraps of conversation, written down on a napkin
body: "...and that's why I never trust a goat."
"Is it supposed to lean like that?" "It's always leaned like that."
"My grandmother swam this. Twice. The second time just to prove the first."
"Look, look — no, you missed it. It was a seal. Or a very wet dog."
"I'll write." "You always say that." "I always mean it."
*At the bottom:* I don't know any of them. I'll miss them anyway.

letters.title: Grandad's Knots
letters.form: Instructions, with careful little drawings of rope
body: **Three knots Grandad says everyone should know**
**The bowline.** The rabbit comes out of the hole, round the tree, and back down the hole. *(Grandad says the rabbit is the most important part.)*
**The clove hitch.** For tying a boat to a post when you mean to come back soon.
**The reef knot.** For tying two things together that should stay together. Right over left, left over right.
*In a different hand, very shaky:* And the fourth, which isn't a knot: always leave a little slack. For the tide. For people.

letters.title: On Behalf of the Gull
letters.form: Short letter, a reply to 12, the handwriting suspiciously human
body: To the writer of the letter to the gull,
The gull has received your letter. The gull has asked me to say that he is not sorry about the sandwich.
The gull would like it known that the sandwich was unattended, and that he regards an unattended sandwich as a kind of invitation.
The gull sends his regards, and will see you on Thursday.
Yours, his secretary

letters.title: Postcard, No Picture
letters.form: Postcard, the picture side washed blank
body: Having a lovely time. The picture was of the harbor, but the sea wanted it, so you'll have to imagine it.
Imagine boats. Imagine the light going gold. Imagine me eating something I shouldn't, with my shoes off.
That's about it. Wish you were here, but I'm glad you're there, keeping things.

letters.title: After the Wedding
letters.form: A thank-you card, a reply to 26
body: Thank you for coming, all of you, and to everyone who couldn't.

The tide was late, so the wedding was late. We stood on the sand in our good shoes and waited for the water to arrive, and nobody minded. A little girl said "the sea is the bride" and we have decided she was right.
Somebody's hat blew away during the vows. It's probably on its way to you now. If so, it's a gift.
With love, and sand in everything,
the two of us

letters.title: The Bread on the Step
letters.form: Short confession, a reply to 24, flour on the paper
body: To the chapel, who asked:
It's me with the bread. I can't tell you who I am, because then it would be a thing, and I'd have to keep doing it properly, and some weeks the loaves come out flat.
I started after my wife died. She baked every Friday and I didn't know what to do with Fridays.
Now I do.
I won't stop. Thank you for asking me not to.

letters.title: Tuesdays
letters.form: Letter, a reply to 24, written in a hurry
body: To whoever is reading the Courier's old columns:
I answered the advertisement about the stubborn old man and the swimming. That was three summers ago.
He floats now. On his back, with his eyes closed and his arms out, and he says it's the first time in his life he hasn't been holding something up.
He still won't put his face in. We're working on it. Tuesdays.
The biscuits are excellent. That part of the advertisement was entirely true.

letters.title: Inventory, Small Boat

2 oars (one good, one opinionated)

letters.title: A Round for Three Voices
letters.form: A song written out by hand, with the entries marked 1, 2 and 3
body: *Sing it through, then start again when the voice before you reaches the second line.*
**1.** Row the boat out past the light,
**2.** leave the harbor, leave the night,
**3.** row it home when morning's white,
and the fire will still be bright.

*At the bottom:* We sang this on the quay every winter until there were too few of us for three parts. Now there's one of me. Sing it for me, if you can find two others. If you can't, sing it anyway and let the waves take the other parts. They always knew them.

letters.title: House Rules
letters.form: A list, crayon, every letter a different color
body: **RULES OF OUR HOUSE**
1. no shoes on the good rug
2. the dog is allowed on the good rug
3. say goodnight to the sea
4. if you find a crab put it back where it was, it has a family
5. pancakes on sundays and also on any day it rains
6. it is allowed to be sad sometimes
7. everyone gets a hug even Uncle Tam

letters.title: Correction
letters.form: Newspaper clipping, a single small paragraph
body: **THE LOWMARSH COURIER**
### CORRECTION
In last week's letters page we described a heron on the old quay as "unusually polite". The heron has since taken a fish directly from Mr. Garrow's bucket while making eye contact.
The Courier regrets the error and stands by the heron's general manners, which remain better than most.

letters.title: Pressed
letters.form: A note folded round a pressed sea pink, which has kept its color
body: There's a sea pink in here. I picked it on the cliff the morning we said goodbye, and pressed it in the dictionary under "P", because I couldn't think of a better word for it.
It's been there long enough. Plant it, if it'll grow. If it won't, just look at it a while. That's what it was for.

letters.title: Two Hundred Words About the Sea
letters.form: Writing exercise, lined paper, a word count in the corner
body: **Two hundred words about the sea**
The sea is big. The sea is wet. The sea is blue except when it is green or grey or the color of the inside of a shell.
My dad says the sea is never the same twice. I asked how he knows and he said he has been checking every morning for forty years.
I tried to count the waves but they don't stop for you to count them.
I think the sea is like a dog that is too big for the house. You love it but you cannot keep it inside.
*Word count: 96*
*In red:* A little short. Everything you said was true. Keep going.

letters.title: Eleven
body: I count the waves in
lose my place at eleven
start again, gladly

letters.title: If This Floats
letters.form: A strip of paper rolled very tight
body: If this floats, Mira owes me a biscuit.
If you're reading it, it floated.
Please tell Mira.

letters.title: Quay Rhyme
letters.form: A skipping rhyme, written down by someone who wanted to keep it
body: *The children on the quay skip to this. I've never heard it anywhere else.*
High tide, low tide,
where did all the fishes hide?
Under the boat, under the stone,
under the jetty, all alone.
One for the heron, two for the gull,
three for the keeper, and the net is full!
*On "full" everyone jumps at once, and whoever lands last has to be the heron.*

letters.title: Not Sent
letters.form: A letter, crossed out and rewritten many times, finished at last
body: Dear —
~~I'm sorry I~~ ~~I should have~~ ~~You were right about~~
I've written this letter nine times. I was going to post it to you, but I think the truth is that it was never really for you. It was for me, to find out what I meant.
What I meant was: thank you. For the years, and for the end of them, which you did more kindly than I did.
I'm giving it to the sea instead. It's better at carrying things than I am.
Be well. Be happy. I mean that, all nine times.

letters.title: Saltbarrow, the Last Page
letters.form: The final page of the same keeper's book, the binding thread still attached
body: **Keeper's Log — Saltbarrow Light**
**30th.** The men came to fit the new lamp. It lights itself now, and turns itself off at dawn, and does not need anybody.
**31st.** Packed. Not much. A kettle, the good knife, this book.
Went down to the lower rocks to say goodbye. All three were there. Councillor looked at me a long while, the way he does, and then went back to sleep in the sun.
Lit the lamp one last time by hand, though it didn't need me to. That's the job. That was always the job.
*Last line, smaller:* Somebody, somewhere, look after something. It's the best way I know to spend a life.

letters.title: The Weather Inside
letters.form: Short note on the back of a ferry ticket
body: Storm outside all day. Inside: one lamp, one cat, one good book, soup.
I used to think a good life was a big one. Now I think it might be this, repeated.

letters.title: From the Island Past the Reef
letters.form: Letter, unsigned, on the same heavy paper as before, now gone soft with salt
body: To whoever tends the next island, again,
The pine is still stubborn. I am still bad at this. Both of these things are going well.

There are three plants here now, and a frog, who arrived on his own one night and has been unimpressed with me ever since. I've built nothing. I've mostly sat. I'm learning that sitting is most of it.
Sometimes on clear evenings I can see your island from the point. Just a dark shape, and once, I think, a little fire.
I wave. You won't see it. Wave back anyway.
